background.definition: The American Urologic Association guideline uses a definition that includes distress to either partner or ejaculation that occurs before it is desired. See for specific subtypes of premature ejaculation.

list.listitem: Premature ejaculation is a common complaint among men. However, true lifelong premature ejaculation is less common, and is thought to be present in 2% to 5% of men.
The etiology of premature ejaculation is uncertain, but it is thought to be a combination of organic and psychological factors, along with negative conditioning and hypersensitivity of the penis.
Ejaculation dysfunction is common in men with schizophrenia.
Low serotonergic neurotransmission has a direct relationship with premature ejaculation and low threshold IELT, 5-HT2c receptor hyposensitivity, and/or 5-HT1a receptor hypersensitivity.
Leptin shows promise of being a marker for premature ejaculation.
The ventral medial preoptic area in the rosthal hypothalamus and nucleus paragigantocellularis medulla are involved in the ejaculation process.
An intravaginal ejaculatory latency time (IELT) between 1 and 2 minutes is diagnostic of premature ejaculation. C
Having 15 or fewer penile thrusts before ejaculation is also diagnostic. C

In men with acquired premature ejaculation, consider the following tests to rule out secondary causes: urinalysis and urine culture to rule out infection and thyrotrophin-stimulating hormone (TSH) to rule out thyroid problems. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Rapid ejaculation with one partner and not another
Low frequency of sexual intercourse and show depressive symptoms
Negative sexual desire, erectile dysfunction, premature ejaculation, and pain

list.listitem: The Fifth Edition of Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders is proposing 4 premature ejaculation categories: lifelong premature ejaculation, acquired premature ejaculation, natural variable premature ejaculation, and premature-like ejaculatory dysfunction ().
Each of the above will differ in ejaculation time course, pattern and frequency of complaint, and its life course.
All 4 of these categories has a low positive predictive value with a high associated risk for a false-positive diagnosis.
The diagnosis is primarily clinical. Office evaluation should take place in a quiet space where questions can be asked in a nonjudgmental way that decreases further embarrassment.

Ask about the time course, onset, and frequency to determine the type of premature ejaculation (). An IELT between 1 minute and 2 minutes is diagnostic of premature ejaculation. Having 15 or fewer penile thrusts before ejaculation is also diagnostic of premature ejaculation.

In clinical practice, it is not practical to evaluate the IELT with a stop watch. A self-estimated time is used and seems to be quite accurate. The clinician must also assess distress, lack of control over ejaculation, sexual satisfaction, intrapersonal difficulty, and persistence.

The Arabic Index of Premature Ejaculation is a 7-item survey with five categories per response. It is used to diagnose the presence of premature ejaculation and its severity, but is primarily useful for research and perhaps monitoring patient response to treatment.
Premature ejaculation is a clinical diagnosis; diagnostic testing is generally not required.
In men with acquired premature ejaculation, consider the following tests to rule out secondary causes: urinalysis and urine culture to rule out infection and TSH to rule out thyroid problems.
In a study of 620 Dutch men, there was no association between thyroid function and ejaculatory function in men with lifelong premature ejaculation.
An IELT between 1 and 2 minutes or having 15 or fewer penile thrusts before ejaculation are diagnostic of premature ejaculation.
Consider medications for patients with lifelong premature ejaculation; they may be taken daily or taken on demand. Options include an SSRI or a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (PDE5-I).
In acquired premature ejaculation, when the etiology is removed but premature ejaculation continues, consider medical therapy.
SSRIs are effective and may be taken daily or on demand. If taken on demand, the medication should have an onset within a few hours, few side effects, and be be effective from the first dose. B
Nonselective alpha-1-receptor blockers are effective in treating premature ejaculation. B
PDE5-Is are effective in treating sexual dysfunction and premature ejaculation. A
TEMPE is a novel aerosol-delivery spray of lidocaine-prilocaine. It is used for on-demand treatment and has fewer side effects than oral treatment. B
Medical therapy is an option for patients with lifelong premature ejaculation, and for those with acquired premature ejaculation who have not improved following treatment of the underlying disorder.

Although not US Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved, SSRIs have been used to treat premature ejaculation. However, there is no universal agreement about dosage or protocol. Drugs may be taken daily, then taken on demand, or only taken daily, or only taken on demand. One study showed men preferred daily dosing, allowing more preferred spontaneous sexual activity. If on demand is chosen, the medication should have an onset within a few hours, have few side effects, and it should be effective from the first dose (see ).
Paroxitene may be more effective than fluoxetine and escitalopram.

Dapoxetine is a short-acting SSRI that can be taken 1 to 3 hours before sexual activity and has been shown to have a 2-minute ejaculation delay. But it has been rejected by the FDA as a treatment for premature ejaculation.

TEMPE is a novel aerosol-delivery spray of lidocaine-prilocaine. It has optimal tissue penetration, rapid onset, no condom is required, and only the mucosa of the penis (not the skin) is anesthetized. It is used for on-demand treatment and has fewer side effects than oral treatment. Treatment increased IELT to 3.8 minutes. It also resulted in positive trends in ejaculatory control. It is easy to use and well tolerated. It seems to work by decreasing the heightened sensitivity of the penis.
Though it remains a treatment option, applying EMLA cream to the penis takes 20 to 30 minutes to work, is messy, a condom must be used, and the whole penis is anesthetized.

Tramadol is a centrally acting synthetic opioid analgesic. The mode of action is not well understood but it may be effective in the treatment of premature ejaculation. It has a potential for addiction.
The nonselective alpha-1-receptor blockers phenoxybenzamine, alfuzosine, and terazosine have been shown to be effective in treating premature ejaculation.

The PDE5-Is sildenafil, vardenafil, and tadalafil are effective for patients with erectile dysfunction and premature ejaculation. By prolonging the erection, they allow a better experience for both partners even if ejaculation occurs early during intercourse.
5-HT(2) antagonists and 5-HT/noradaeniline reuptake inhibitors are not effective in treating premature ejaculation.

Psychotherapy is recommended for patients with acquired premature ejaculation (particularly if there is a relationship problem or issue), as well as for patients with premature-like ejaculatory dysfunction.
There is weak evidence for psychosocial interventions for premature ejaculation.

Female sexual dysfunction is directly associated with male partner premature ejaculation. The male frequently has anxiety, reduced self-esteem, depression, embarrassment, and relationship problems. Therefore, consider family counseling and couples therapy.
Patients with natural variable premature ejaculation need reassurance and education about what is normal.
Patients with premature-like ejaculatory dysfunction generally require psychotherapy and/or counseling.
Lifelong or primary premature ejaculation has a poor prognosis. It may require lifetime medication and counseling. C
Acquired premature ejaculation has a mixed prognosis, depending on comorbidities, stressors, and psychological sequalae. C

feature.caption: Different Types of Premature Ejaculation.
feature.feature_body:
Type Characteristics Treatment
Lifelong premature ejaculation Occurs with nearly every intercourse and with every woman, from first sexual encounter onward Medication
Acquired premature ejaculation This begins at some point in a man's life, following normal ejaculation to that point. May be caused by a physical (thyroid, prostatitis, erectile dysfunction) or a psychological problem Medication and/or psychotherapy
Natural variable premature ejaculation This is a situational problem that occurs inconsistently or irregularly. More of a normal variant than a pathologic diagnosis Reassurance
Premature-like ejaculatory dysfunction Ejaculation time is in the normal range (ie, 3-6 minutes) and may be of very long duration. However, patient perceives that this is early or that they do not control ejaculation Reassurance or psychotherapy
Waldinger MD. Premature ejaculation: different pathophysiologies and etiologies determine its treatment. J Sex Marital Ther 2008;34:1-13.
